lessons.title: Understanding Snail Mating and Reproductive Cycles
lessons.body:
Snails are hermaphrodites, meaning each snail has both male and female reproductive organs. However, most species cannot self-fertilize; they need a partner to exchange sperm. In Africa, the most farmed species is the giant African land snail (Achatina achatina, Achatina fulica, and Archachatina marginata). These snails reach sexual maturity at about 6 to 12 months, depending on species and feeding. For example, Achatina achatina matures around 10-12 months, while Archachatina marginata may mature at 8-10 months. You can tell a snail is mature when the lip of its shell thickens and curls outward, a condition called the 'lip'.

Mating usually occurs at night or early morning, especially after rain. The snail will climb on another, and they align their bodies so their genital pores meet. Sperm exchange can take several hours. After mating, sperm is stored in the recipient's body for weeks or months. The snail then lays eggs when conditions are right. In warm, humid climates, mating can happen year-round, but peaks during the rainy season.

Egg-laying follows 8 to 20 days after mating. A snail digs a hole in moist soil, usually 2-5 cm deep, and lays a clutch of eggs. Clutch size varies: Achatina fulica can lay 100-400 eggs per clutch, while Archachatina marginata lays 20-70 eggs. The eggs are white or yellowish, oval, and about 4-6 mm in diameter. The snail covers the hole with soil and leaves. A single snail can lay 3-6 clutches per year.

To manage breeding, keep a ratio of 2 females to 1 male? Actually, since they are hermaphrodites, any two snails can mate. But for good fertility, stock at least 10-20 snails per square meter in a breeding pen. Provide a substrate of loose, moist soil (not waterlogged) mixed with calcium sources like crushed eggshells or limestone. Keep temperature between 22-28Â°C and humidity at 70-90%. In dry areas, mist the pen daily. Observe mating and egg-laying to plan your production cycle. Remove eggs carefully to incubate separately, or leave them in the soil if you want natural hatching. But for higher survival, collect and incubate. This understanding helps you time your breeding and maximize output.

lessons.title: Selecting Breeding Stock for Health and Productivity
lessons.body:
Choosing the right breeding stock is the foundation of a profitable snail farm. Start by selecting snails that are healthy, active, and have a good shell shape. Avoid snails with cracked, thin, or discolored shells, as these may indicate poor nutrition or disease. Look for snails that are alert, with tentacles extended, and that move quickly when touched. A healthy snail retracts into its shell and then comes out again within a minute or two. Sluggish snails may be sick or stressed.

Size matters. For breeding, choose the largest and fastest-growing snails from your batch. In Archachatina marginata, a good breeder should have a shell length of at least 10-12 cm. For Achatina achatina, aim for 12-15 cm. Larger snails tend to lay more eggs and produce stronger offspring. Also, select snails with a thick, glossy shell and a well-formed lip, indicating maturity. Do not breed snails younger than 8 months; their eggs may be small and fewer.

Source your stock from reputable farms or from the wild if you can ensure they are not exposed to pesticides. In Africa, many farmers collect from the bush during the rainy season. But wild snails may carry parasites. Quarantine new snails for 2-3 weeks in a separate pen, feeding them clean food and observing for illness. Treat with a mild salt bath? No, salt is harmful. Instead, use a dilute potassium permanganate solution (0.1%) to dip snails for 1-2 minutes to kill external parasites. Then rinse with clean water.

Record keeping is key. Tag or mark your breeders with a small dot of non-toxic paint on the shell, or keep them in separate pens. Track each snail's egg-laying performance. A good breeder lays at least 3 clutches per year with 80% fertility. Cull snails that consistently lay few eggs or have poor hatch rates. Replace breeders every 12-18 months to maintain vigor. Inbreeding leads to weak offspring, so introduce new blood every 2-3 generations. Exchange males with other farmers or buy new stock annually.

Feed breeders a high-protein diet: pawpaw leaves, cabbage, carrot, and formulated feed with 16-18% protein. Add calcium (crushed oyster shell or limestone) ad libitum. Keep breeding pens clean and at optimal temperature (24-28Â°C) and humidity (75-85%). With careful selection, you can increase egg production by 30-50% within a year.

lessons.title: Creating Optimal Conditions for Egg Laying
lessons.body:
To get snails to lay eggs, you must mimic their natural environment. The most critical factors are soil, moisture, temperature, and calcium. Snails lay eggs in moist, loose soil. Use a substrate of loamy soil mixed with peat moss or coconut coir. The soil should be at least 10-15 cm deep to allow digging. Sterilize the soil before use by spreading it under the sun for 2-3 days or baking it in an oven at 80Â°C for 30 minutes to kill pests and pathogens. Mix in crushed eggshells or agricultural lime at 10% by volume to provide calcium for eggshell formation.

Moisture is crucial. The substrate should be damp but not waterloggedâlike a wrung-out sponge. If you squeeze a handful, no water should drip out. Aim for 70-80% humidity in the air. In dry African climates, mist the pen twice daily with a hand sprayer. You can also place a shallow dish of water in the pen for snails to drink, but they mostly get moisture from food and soil. Avoid standing water, which breeds bacteria and drowns snails.

Temperature should be between 22-28Â°C. In hot regions, provide shade with palm fronds or shade netting. In cooler highlands, use a greenhouse or polythene tunnel to keep warmth. Snails are nocturnal; they lay eggs mostly at night. Provide hiding places like broken pots, coconut shells, or pieces of wood. This reduces stress and encourages breeding. Keep the pen quiet and free from ants, rats, and birds, which eat eggs and young snails.

Diet also affects egg laying. Feed breeders a mix of fresh vegetables (cabbage, lettuce, cucumber), fruits (pawpaw, mango, banana), and a protein supplement like soybean meal or fish meal. Add calcium-rich foods: crushed oyster shells, limestone, or even ground bone meal. A good laying diet has 16-18% protein and 4-5% calcium. Feed once daily in the evening. Remove uneaten food the next morning to prevent mold.

Finally, manage snail density. Overcrowding causes stress and reduces egg laying. Keep 10-15 adult snails per square meter in breeding pens. Provide a 1:1 ratio of males to females? Since they are hermaphrodites, any two can mate, but more snails increase chances. Observe for mating and egg-laying. When you see a snail digging, it may be about to lay. Do not disturb. After laying, the snail covers the hole. You can leave the eggs in the soil for natural hatching, but for higher survival, carefully dig them up after 24 hours and transfer to an incubator. With these conditions, your snails will lay consistently, and you can collect eggs every 2-3 months.

lessons.title: Incubating and Hatching Snail Eggs
lessons.body:
Once you collect snail eggs, you need to incubate them to ensure high hatch rates. Natural hatching in the soil can be as low as 30-50% due to predators and moisture problems. With proper incubation, you can achieve 80-95% hatchability. Collect eggs carefully. After a snail lays, wait 24-48 hours for the eggs to harden slightly. Then gently dig them up with a small spoon or your fingers. Place them in a clean container with moist substrate. Do not wash the eggs; they have a protective coating.

For incubation, use a plastic container with a lid. Make small holes in the lid for ventilation. Fill the container with 3-5 cm of sterile, moist substrate: coconut coir, peat moss, or fine sand mixed with soil. The substrate should be damp but not wet. Place the eggs gently on the surface, not buried deep. You can leave them slightly exposed. Cover the container with the lid, but ensure air exchange. Keep the container in a dark, warm place at 24-28Â°C. A cupboard or a shaded shelf works. Do not put in direct sunlight.

Check the substrate moisture daily. If it feels dry, mist lightly with a spray bottle. Never pour water directly on eggs. Humidity should be around 80-90%. You can also place a small dish of water inside the incubator to maintain humidity. Eggs usually hatch in 14-30 days, depending on species and temperature. Achatina fulica hatches in 14-21 days; Archachatina marginata in 21-30 days. You will see tiny snails emerging with their shells. They are about 2-3 mm in size.

Once hatched, leave the hatchlings in the incubator for 2-3 days to absorb the yolk sac. Then transfer them to a nursery pen. Do not handle them with your fingers; use a soft brush or a spoon. The nursery pen should have the same conditions as the incubator: moist substrate, 24-28Â°C, high humidity. Feed them finely ground food: grated carrot, pawpaw leaf, and a calcium source like powdered eggshell. Keep the nursery clean and free from ants.

For best results, incubate eggs in small batches and label with date and parent stock. Record hatch rates. If you notice mold on eggs, remove them immediately. Mold indicates too much moisture or poor ventilation. With practice, you can hatch hundreds of snails per month, providing stock for your grow-out pens or for sale. Remember, snail eggs are fragile; handle with care.

lessons.title: Rearing Hatchlings: Nursery Management
lessons.body:
Hatchlings are tiny and vulnerable. The first 4-8 weeks are critical for survival. A well-managed nursery can achieve 90% survival, while neglect can lead to 50% or more mortality. Prepare the nursery before eggs hatch. Use a clean plastic tray or wooden box with a lid. Line it with 2-3 cm of moist, sterile substrate (coconut coir or fine soil). Add a thin layer of crushed eggshell or limestone powder for calcium. The nursery should be kept at 24-28Â°C and 80-90% humidity. In dry conditions, cover the tray with a damp cloth or plastic sheet with holes.

When hatchlings emerge, they are about the size of a pinhead. Do not touch them. Leave them in the incubator for 2-3 days until they start moving around. Then transfer them gently using a soft brush or a piece of lettuce leaf. Place them in the nursery at a density of 50-100 hatchlings per square meter. Overcrowding causes stress and stunted growth. As they grow, reduce density to 20-30 per square meter by 4 weeks.

Feed hatchlings a finely ground diet. Use a blender or mortar to grind dried leaves (pawpaw, cabbage, lettuce), vegetables (carrot, cucumber), and a protein source (soybean meal, fish meal). Add calcium powder. Feed small amounts twice dailyâmorning and evening. Remove leftovers to prevent mold. Hatchlings also need moisture; mist the substrate lightly daily. Never let it dry out completely. Provide a shallow water dish with a stone for them to climb on, but ensure they don't drown.

Keep the nursery dark and quiet. Snails are nocturnal and shy. Avoid direct sunlight and loud noises. Protect from ants, which can kill hatchlings. Place the nursery legs in moats of water or use ant powder around the perimeter (but not inside). Check daily for dead snails and remove them immediately. Also watch for mites or small flies; if seen, clean the nursery and replace substrate.

After 4-6 weeks, hatchlings are about 1-2 cm and can be moved to grow-out pens. Before transfer, acclimate them by placing the nursery near the grow-out pen for a day. Then introduce them at a density of 10-15 per square meter. Continue feeding a high-protein diet. With proper nursery management, you can raise strong, healthy snails that reach market size in 8-12 months. Record growth rates and select the fastest growers for future breeding.

lessons.title: Genetic Selection and Improving Stock Quality
lessons.body:
Genetic selection is how you improve your snail farm over time. Without it, your snails may become smaller, slower-growing, and more disease-prone. The goal is to select for traits that increase profit: fast growth, large size, high egg production, and disease resistance. Start by identifying your best performers. Keep records for each breeding snail: date of hatching, growth rate (weight at 3, 6, 9 months), number of eggs laid per clutch, hatch rate, and survival of offspring. Use a simple notebook or spreadsheet.

Select breeders from the top 20% of your stock. For example, if you have 100 snails, choose the 20 largest and fastest-growing as future breeders. Also, select for shell quality: thick, smooth, and well-formed. Avoid snails with deformities. In Archachatina marginata, aim for shell length of 12-14 cm at 12 months. In Achatina achatina, 14-16 cm. For egg production, choose snails that lay at least 4 clutches per year with 80% hatch rate. Cull snails that lay fewer than 2 clutches or have poor hatch rates.

Inbreeding is a major problem. If you breed siblings or close relatives, you get weak offspring, lower fertility, and higher mortality. To avoid this, introduce new blood every 2-3 generations. You can exchange breeding snails with other farmers, or buy from a reputable source. When introducing new snails, quarantine them for 3 weeks before adding to your breeding pen. Keep a breeding chart to track lineages. Use different colored tags to mark families.

You can also practice line breeding: select a male and female from different families with desired traits and breed them. Then select the best offspring from that cross. This is called outcrossing. Over time, you can develop your own improved line. Another technique is to select for early maturity. Snails that mature at 6 months instead of 12 months can produce more generations per year, accelerating genetic gain. But ensure they are healthy and not stunted.

Finally, manage your environment to allow genetic potential to express. Even the best genetics will fail with poor feed, dirty pens, or stress. Provide optimal conditions as covered in earlier lessons. Keep detailed records and review them every 6 months. Replace breeders annually. With consistent selection, you can increase average snail size by 10-20% per year and egg production by 20-30%. This leads to higher profits and a sustainable snail farming business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Snail Breeding, Reproduction & Stock Improvement

In African heliciculture, the breeding unit is the profit engine of the farm. Every hatchling you produce internally saves cash that would otherwise leave the business as purchase cost, and every gram of growth you capture through better genetics compounds across hundreds of snails. This reference module gives you the operating parameters, records discipline and selection logic you need to move from "keeping snails" to running a productive breeding programme. It is written for the West African giant land snail (Achatina achatina), the favoured commercial species in Ghana, Nigeria and CÃ´te d'Ivoire, with notes on Achatina fulica and Archachatina marginata where behaviour differs.

Treat breeding as a cost centre with a measurable output: sellable juveniles per breeder per cycle. If a pen of 100 breeders yields 3,000 healthy hatchlings reaching 5 g in 90 days, your unit economics work. If it yields 300, the same feed, labour and housing are spread over a tenth of the revenue. The difference is almost never luck â it is stock selection, moisture control, calcium supply and hygiene.

Understanding Mating and the Reproductive Cycle

Giant land snails are hermaphrodites: each mature individual carries both male and female organs, but cross-fertilisation is the norm. Mating is reciprocal â both partners exchange sperm and both can subsequently lay eggs. This is a critical business insight: you do not need a 1:1 male-to-female ratio, and you cannot assume a snail that mated once will not lay. A single pairing can fertilise multiple clutches over several months because sperm is stored in the spermatheca.

Sexual maturity in A. achatina typically arrives at 8â12 months under good management, signalled by a thickened, flared shell lip (the "lip" or peristome). Mating is triggered by rising humidity at the onset of the rains. In a controlled pen you simulate this with a wet-season misting cycle. Courtship can last 2â6 hours; egg laying follows 8â20 days later. Clutches range from 80 to 300 eggs depending on species, size and nutrition, buried 3â6 cm in loose, moist soil.

Selecting Breeding Stock

Do not breed from the first snails that reach size. Select deliberately, and cull hard. Poor breeders are the single largest hidden cost in small African snail farms because they consume feed and occupy pen space while producing weak or no clutches.

Selection criteria, in order of commercial importance:

  • Shell health: smooth, well-coloured, no cracks, no thin or translucent patches (a calcium-deficiency signal you do not want to propagate).
  • Body mass: heavy, well-filled foot; in A. achatina breeders should be at least 120â180 g at first mating.
  • Growth rate: use your own records â snails that reached 100 g fastest are your genetic winners.
  • Lip development: a thick, flared lip confirms maturity; breeding immature snails wastes cycles.
  • Activity: responsive to touch, active at dusk, good feeding response.
  • Proven performance: in a second cycle, retain only snails that laid large clutches and hatched well.

Maintain a breeding ratio of roughly 1:1 to 2:1 (any combination works since all are hermaphrodites, but density matters more than ratio). Replace breeders after 2â3 laying cycles â productivity declines and shell wear increases. Keep a separate "elite" pen of your top 10â15% performers to push the genetics forward each generation.

Sources: Cobbinah, Vink & Onwuka (2008), Snail Farming: Production, Processing and Marketing, Agromisa Agrodok 47; FAO (1990), Manual on the Production of Snails; FAO (2013), Snail Farming in West Africa: A Guide for Farmers.

Creating Optimal Conditions for Egg Laying

Egg laying is triggered by moisture, not by feed. Breeders will hold eggs and reabsorb or abort them if the substrate is too dry or waterlogged. Target soil moisture at "squeeze test" level: a handful of soil holds together when squeezed but no water drips out â roughly 70â80% field capacity.

Provide a dedicated laying tray or zone: 8â12 cm of loose, friable loam, sieved to remove stones, mixed with sieved compost or coir. Keep it shaded at 24â28 Â°C. In hot northern Nigerian or Sahelian conditions, mist twice daily during the laying window and cover pens with shade netting or palm fronds. In humid forest zones (Ghana, Cross River, CÃ´te d'Ivoire), watch for waterlogging â add coarse sand or raise the tray.

Calcium is non-negotiable. Supply ground oyster shell, limestone grit or powdered eggshell ad libitum alongside feed. A calcium-deficient breeder lays thin-shelled eggs that collapse, or stops laying entirely. Feed breeders a mixed ration of pawpaw leaf, cocoyam leaf, sweet potato leaf, ripe fruit (pawpaw, mango, banana) and a supplementary mash (maize bran, soybean meal, groundnut cake, limestone, vitamin premix).

Incubating and Hatching Eggs

Collect clutches carefully with a plastic spoon â never bare fingers, which transfer oils and salt. Transfer to labelled incubation trays: plastic basins or wooden boxes with 6â8 cm of sterilised, moistened soil or coir. Cover with a breathable cloth or perforated lid to hold humidity while allowing air exchange.

Do not turn the eggs. Keep them in the dark. Check moisture every 2 days by misting lightly if the surface dries. At 24â28 Â°C, A. achatina eggs hatch in 21â28 days. Hatchlings emerge with a soft, translucent shell and immediately seek calcium â provide crushed shell or cuttlebone in the nursery from day one.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chemical and biological hazards

Never use agricultural pesticides, insecticides or herbicides in or near snail pens. Snails absorb chemicals through the foot and mantle and will die, and residue makes the meat unsafe for sale and consumption. Similarly, do not use unwashed poultry manure or fresh animal waste as pen substrate â it carries Salmonella, E. coli and parasite eggs that can transfer to the meat. Compost manure fully (minimum 6â8 weeks, turned weekly) before use, or use coir/loam only. Always wash hands and tools after handling snails or substrate, and never allow children to handle breeders unsupervised. Snails sold for export must meet EU/African market residue and microbiological standards â chemical contamination can destroy a whole season's contract.

Rearing Hatchlings: Nursery Management

The first 60 days determine your survival rate. Hatchlings are fragile: they lose moisture fast, drown easily, and are crushed by adults. Move them to a dedicated nursery pen â shallow trays (10â15 cm deep) with 3â5 cm of moist coir, a fine mesh lid, and no adults.

Stocking density at nursery stage: 200â400 hatchlings per square metre for the first month, then thin to 100â150 per mÂ² by week 6. Overcrowding causes stunted growth, shell damage and disease. Feed finely ground leaves (pawpaw, lettuce, cocoyam) plus a calcium source and a starter mash. Mist daily; maintain 75â85% relative humidity. Keep temperature 24â28 Â°C and out of direct sun.

Expected performance under good management: 80â90% survival to 60 days, average weight 2â5 g. Anything below 70% survival means you have a moisture, density or calcium problem â diagnose before scaling up.

Sources: FAO (1990) Manual on the Production of Snails; Cobbinah et al. (2008) Agrodok 47; field benchmarks from Ghana and Nigeria snail farmer extension programmes (MoFA Ghana, 2015).

Genetic Selection and Improving Stock Quality

Most African snail farms never improve their stock â they breed whatever survives. That is a business mistake. Even modest selection over 3â4 generations can raise growth rate by 15â25% and clutch size by 10â20%, which directly reduces your cost per kilogram of saleable snail.

Practical selection protocol:

  1. Tag and record: number your breeder pens and track each cohort's hatch date, parent weight, clutch size, hatch rate and 90-day weight.
  2. Select the top 15â20% by growth rate and clutch size as next-generation breeders.
  3. Avoid inbreeding: rotate breeders between pens and, where possible, introduce unrelated stock from a trusted farm every 3â4 generations.
  4. Cull ruthlessly: remove slow growers, cracked shells, and any snail showing disease or deformity. Sell culls as meat â do not breed them.
  5. Keep an elite line separate from the commercial line so you always have clean genetics to fall back on.

Record-keeping is the entire foundation. A simple notebook or spreadsheet with columns for pen ID, hatch date, breeder weights, clutch size, hatch rate and 90-day weight is enough to drive real genetic gain. Without records, selection is guesswork.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Breeders at least 8â12 months old, 120â180 g, thick flared lip â never breed immature snails.
  • â Substrate moisture at squeeze-test level (70â80% field capacity); mist twice daily in hot zones.
  • â Calcium source (oyster shell / limestone / eggshell) available ad libitum at all stages.
  • â Laying trays 8â12 cm deep, sieved loam/coir, shaded at 24â28 Â°C.
  • â Collect eggs with a spoon, never fingers; incubate in dark, moist trays; do not turn eggs.
  • â Move hatchlings to a dedicated nursery within 48 hours; thin density by week 6.
  • â Record every cohort: hatch date, clutch size, hatch rate, 90-day weight.
  • â Select top 15â20% as next breeders; cull slow growers and deformed shells; rotate genetics to avoid inbreeding.
  • â No pesticides, no fresh manure, wash hands and tools after every handling session.

quiz.q: What does it mean that snails are hermaphrodites?
options: B) They have both male and female reproductive organs
quiz.explanation: Hermaphrodites have both male and female reproductive organs, but most snails still need a partner to exchange sperm.

quiz.q: At what age do giant African land snails typically reach sexual maturity?
quiz.explanation: Most species mature between 6 and 12 months, depending on species and feeding.

quiz.q: Which species of snail is commonly farmed in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Achatina achatina, along with Achatina fulica and Archachatina marginata, are the main farmed species in Africa.

quiz.q: How can you tell a snail is mature?
options: A) It has a thick, curled lip on its shell
D) It has a shiny shell
quiz.explanation: The thickening and curling of the shell lip, called the 'lip', indicates sexual maturity.

quiz.q: What is the typical clutch size for Achatina fulica?
quiz.explanation: Achatina fulica can lay 100-400 eggs per clutch, while Archachatina marginata lays fewer.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of snails in a breeding pen?
quiz.explanation: A density of 10-20 adult snails per square meter is optimal for breeding.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a healthy breeding snail?
options: A) It retracts and stays in its shell
C) It moves quickly when touched
D) It has a cracked shell
quiz.explanation: Healthy snails are alert and move quickly when touched, while sluggish snails may be sick.

quiz.q: Why should you quarantine new snails before adding them to your breeding pen?
options: A) To prevent them from mating too soon
B) To observe for illness and parasites
C) To help them adapt to new food
D) To make them grow faster
quiz.explanation: Quarantine for 2-3 weeks helps identify and treat any diseases or parasites before introduction.

quiz.q: What is the best way to mark breeding snails for record keeping?
options: A) Cut a notch in the shell
B) Use a non-toxic paint dot on the shell
C) Tie a string around the shell
D) Write on the shell with permanent marker
quiz.explanation: A small dot of non-toxic paint is safe and easy to identify individual snails.

quiz.q: How often should you replace breeding snails?
quiz.explanation: Replacing breeders every 12-18 months helps maintain vigor and prevents inbreeding.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil depth for snail egg laying?
quiz.explanation: Snails need at least 10-15 cm of loose soil to dig and lay eggs.

quiz.q: How can you sterilize soil for use in snail pens?
options: B) Spread under sun for 2-3 days or bake at 80Â°C for 30 minutes
quiz.explanation: Solarization or baking kills pests and pathogens without harmful chemicals.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity range for snail breeding pens?
quiz.explanation: Snails need high humidity (70-90%) for egg laying and overall health.

quiz.q: What calcium source can be added to snail substrate?
quiz.explanation: Crushed eggshells or limestone provide calcium for eggshell formation and shell growth.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overcrowding in breeding pens?
options: A) It causes stress and reduces egg laying
B) Snails will eat each other
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding stresses snails, leading to lower egg production and higher disease risk.

quiz.q: What is the typical incubation period for Achatina fulica eggs?
quiz.explanation: Achatina fulica eggs hatch in about 14-21 days at optimal temperatures.

quiz.q: How should you handle snail eggs during collection?
options: B) Gently dig with a spoon, do not wash
C) Pick with fingers and rub clean
quiz.explanation: Eggs have a protective coating; washing removes it and can harm the embryo.

quiz.q: What is a suitable incubation substrate?
options: B) Moist coconut coir or peat moss
quiz.explanation: Moist coconut coir or peat moss holds humidity well and is sterile.

quiz.q: What temperature range is best for incubating snail eggs?
quiz.explanation: 24-28Â°C is optimal for embryo development and hatching.

quiz.q: What should you do if mold appears on incubating eggs?
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates excess moisture or poor ventilation; remove affected eggs to prevent spread.

quiz.q: How long should hatchlings stay in the incubator after hatching?
quiz.explanation: Hatchlings absorb the yolk sac for 2-3 days before needing external food.

quiz.q: What is the recommended density for hatchlings in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: 50-100 hatchlings per square meter is ideal initially; reduce as they grow.

quiz.q: What food should be given to hatchlings?
options: B) Finely ground vegetables and calcium powder
quiz.explanation: Hatchlings need finely ground food that is easy to consume and rich in calcium.

quiz.q: How can you protect nursery snails from ants?
options: A) Place legs in water moats
quiz.explanation: Water moats around the nursery prevent ants from reaching the snails without chemicals.

quiz.q: When can hatchlings be moved to grow-out pens?
quiz.explanation: At 4-6 weeks, hatchlings are about 1-2 cm and can survive in grow-out pens.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of genetic selection in snail farming?
options: B) To improve growth, size, and egg production
C) To make snails more aggressive
quiz.explanation: Selection focuses on traits that increase productivity and profitability.

quiz.q: Why is inbreeding harmful in snail breeding?
options: B) It leads to weak offspring and lower fertility
C) It makes snails lay more eggs
quiz.explanation: Inbreeding reduces genetic diversity, causing weaker, less fertile offspring.

quiz.q: How often should you introduce new blood into your breeding stock?
quiz.explanation: Introducing new blood every 2-3 generations prevents inbreeding depression.

quiz.q: What records should you keep for genetic selection?
options: B) Growth rate, egg production, hatch rate, survival
quiz.explanation: Comprehensive records help identify the best performers for breeding.

quiz.q: What is outcrossing?
options: B) Breeding unrelated snails with desired traits
C) Breeding snails with different species
quiz.explanation: Outcrossing introduces new genetic material and can improve vigor and productivity.
